item.title: FAO honors highlight China's efforts to strengthen global food security
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-24
FAO honors highlight China's efforts to strengthen global food security Yin Yuzhen (R), Chinese sand-control pioneer, honoree of Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)'s 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, poses for a photo with Ronald Sakolsky at the FAO's World Food Day ceremony in Rome, Italy, Oct. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Kaiyan) * The recent FAO honors awarded to Chinese desertification control pioneer Yin Yuzhen and a Chinese research institute highlighted China's broader efforts to strengthen global food security through ecological restoration, technological innovation and international cooperation. * Jordan's Princess Basma bint Ali described Yin's decades-long efforts as "the other face of innovation." She stressed that addressing hunger, climate shocks and inequality required sustained attention and action. * Beyond ecological restoration, technological innovation offers another way to strengthen food security, helping countries boost agricultural production, address environmental risks and build more resilient food systems. * In an interview with Xinhua, FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero noted that China had been preparing for natural and geopolitical risks by diversifying imports, keeping its market open and improving stock management. ROME, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- As Chinese desertification control pioneer Yin Yuzhen was honored at the headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Rome, her longtime American friend Ronald Sakolsky looked on, his eyes filled with tears. "Yin deserves everything that she gets. She is the heroine," said Sakolsky, a retired teacher who helped fund her tree-planting efforts more than two decades ago. At the Oct. 15 ceremony, Yin was named among the FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, an initiative marking the International Year of the Woman Farmer 2026. A day later, a Chinese research institute received an FAO award for its crop-monitoring technology. Together, the honors highlighted China's broader efforts to strengthen global food security through ecological restoration, technological innovation and international cooperation. FROM SHIFTING SANDS TO A GREEN LANDSCAPE The story of Yin and Sakolsky began in 1999, when Sakolsky was teaching in central China's Henan Province. After seeing a TV report about Yin's efforts to hold back the encroaching sands in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, he raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support her afforestation endeavor. After losing touch for years, the two reunited in Inner Mongolia in August 2026. By then, the seedlings supported by Sakolsky's donation had grown into more than 50,000 trees. Since planting her first tree in 1986, Yin has helped green over 70,000 mu (around 4,667 hectares) of sandy land, an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches. Today, the area supports a greater variety of crops and plants, including cherries and roses, creating new opportunities for agricultural production and income growth. "I have spent more than 40 years transforming this desert, and now all kinds of food can grow here," Yin told Xinhua. Yin's efforts reflect China's broader push to combat desertification, a major part of which is the Three-North Shelterbelt Forest Program, launched in 1978 to restore degraded land and strengthen ecological security in northern China. For Yin, combating desertification is also essential to agricultural production. "If we cannot control the sand, how can we grow good crops when sandstorms come? How can we improve the soil?" she said. At the World Food Day ceremony in Rome on Oct. 16, Jordan's Princess Basma bint Ali described Yin's decades-long efforts as "the other face of innovation." She stressed that addressing hunger, climate shocks and inequality required sustained attention and action. "It must be the steady kind that plants, tends and finally harvests the gains. As did Yin Yuzhen," the princess said. Director-General of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Qu Dongyu (R) presents the 2026 Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Achievement Award to Wu Bingfang, a researcher at the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS) at the closing ceremony of the World Food Forum, in Rome, Italy, Oct. 16, 2026.(Xinhua/Wang Kaiyan) INNOVATION FOR GLOBAL FOOD SECURITY Beyond ecological restoration, technological innovation offers another way to strengthen food security, helping countries boost agricultural production, address environmental risks and build more resilient food systems. On Oct. 16, the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences received the 2026 FAO Achievement Award for its CropWatch, a cloud-based crop-monitoring platform. Developed by a team led by researcher Wu Bingfang, the platform combines satellite observations with climate and agricultural data to monitor crop conditions, assess production prospects and identify risks such as drought and abnormal rainfall. Through its open cloud service, CropWatch allows users to conduct their own crop assessments without investing heavily in local computing infrastructure. According to the research team, the platform has helped more than 40 countries and regions monitor crop conditions, and its bulletins have served users in 173 countries and regions. CropWatch has also been integrated into the FAO's Hand-in-Hand Geospatial Platform and the Group on Earth Observations Knowledge Hub. It serves as an important channel and an independent source of timely crop monitoring information for users worldwide. Wu told Xinhua after receiving the award that the recognition affirmed the team's more than three decades of dedication. "This is not the end, but a milestone on a new journey ahead," he said. Photo taken on Oct. 16, 2026 shows a general view of the World Food Day ceremony at the headquarter of Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Rome. (Xinhua/Wang Kaiyan) SHARING CHINESE EXPERIENCE FOR FOOD SECURITY China's contribution extends beyond domestic production to international agricultural cooperation. In addition to feeding its own population of more than 1.4 billion, China has also provided assistance to countries in need, contributing to global food security. Zhang Lubiao, China's permanent representative to the FAO, said China would deepen cooperation with the FAO in hybrid rice, water-saving irrigation, digital agriculture and climate-adaptive technologies, among other areas. Such cooperation is already yielding tangible results in various countries. Nosipho Jezile, South Africa's permanent representative to the UN food and agriculture agencies, said China's South-South cooperation projects with the FAO had supported rice cultivation, aquaculture, irrigation infrastructure, mechanization and agricultural innovation in African countries. "These projects have brought tangible increases in output and created employment opportunities," she said. Food security depends on more than agricultural production. Keeping food affordable and ensuring a stable supply of fertilizers and other agricultural inputs are also essential, particularly amid economic and geopolitical uncertainties. In an interview with Xinhua, FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero said rising prices, rather than immediate food shortages, posed the biggest risk to global food security at present. Torero noted that China had been preparing for natural and geopolitical risks by diversifying imports, keeping its market open and improving stock management. China's urea exports were also helping bring down prices, he said, urging major producers and importers not to distort markets or restrict exports of agricultural inputs. item.title: China's top diplomat calls for China-U.S. joint efforts on AI development, governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-24
China's top diplomat calls for China-U.S. joint efforts on AI development, governance XIONGAN, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China and the United States have both the capability and the responsibility to jointly develop and govern artificial intelligence (AI) well, ensuring that its development remains under human control and benefits the people, China's top diplomat Wang Yi said on Friday. "We should not only guard against risks but also engage in cooperation to jointly discuss globally applicable rules and standards so that AI serves to promote common prosperity and safeguard common security," Wang said. China maintains that AI development should be inclusive, beneficial, for the positive and for good, he said. Wang, Chinese foreign minister and a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks during his meeting with co-chair of the Board of Trustees of the Asia Society John L. Thornton and The New York Times columnist Thomas L. Friedman, who are in China for the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan). Noting that the world is currently confronted with multiple governance deficits in areas including peace, development and security, Wang said that in September 2025, President Xi Jinping put forward the Global Governance Initiative, which provided an important public good for the world and received wide recognition and support from the international community. By hosting the global governance forum in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province, China hopes to pool consensus from various parties and jointly promote the reform of the global governance system, Wang added. Thornton and Friedman expressed congratulations on President Xi's successful visit to the United States, hoping that the two countries will enhance cooperation on AI and provide important public goods for the world. They said that the international community is paying close attention to the upcoming APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by China, and expects that China will take this opportunity to play a unique and positive role in tackling global challenges. item.title: China launches new remote sensing satellite
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-24
China launches new remote sensing satellite A modified Long March-6 carrier rocket carrying the Yaogan-50 03 satellite blasts off from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in north China's Shanxi Province, Oct. 23, 2026. The Yaogan-50 03 satellite was launched at 6:15 p.m. (Beijing Time) and entered its planned orbit. The launch mission was a complete success. (Photo by Dong Meng/Xinhua) TAIYUAN, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China launched a remote sensing satellite from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in north China's Shanxi Province on Friday. The Yaogan-50 03 satellite was launched at 6:15 p.m. (Beijing Time) aboard a modified Long March-6 carrier rocket and entered its planned orbit. The launch mission was a complete success. The satellite will mainly be used for land survey, crop yield estimation, and disaster prevention and relief. The launch marked the 672nd flight mission of the Long March carrier rocket series. A modified Long March-6 carrier rocket carrying the Yaogan-50 03 satellite blasts off from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in north China's Shanxi Province, Oct. 23, 2026. item.title: Xi sends message to 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan)
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-24
Xi sends message to 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping sent a message to the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) on Friday. The world is undergoing accelerated transformation unseen in a century, and the deficits in peace, development, security and governance are growing rather than diminishing, Xi said. "I have put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) to promote the building of a more just and equitable global governance system and a better world," he said. China stands ready to work with all parties to uphold the vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, pool strength through confidence-building and tackle challenges through cooperation, Xi said. He called for efforts to promote the implementation of the GGI to inject more certainty and positive energy into a world of turbulence and transformation, and jointly move toward a community with a shared future for humanity. The forum opened on the same day in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province. Hosted by the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs, it is themed "Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Reforming and Improving Global Governance in a Transforming World." item.title: Xi chairs CPC leadership meeting to review disciplinary inspection report
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23
Xi chairs CPC leadership meeting to review disciplinary inspection report BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee held a meeting on Friday to review a report on the seventh round of disciplinary inspection launched by the 20th CPC Central Committee. Xi Jinping, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, chaired the meeting. The meeting hailed the work performance and results of the inspection. According to the inspection results, central Party and government departments have made progress in their work, but some problems still exist and need to be taken seriously. The meeting urged solid efforts to rectify the problems identified by the inspection. It called on central Party and government departments to strengthen their sense of political responsibility in performing their duties, deepen reform, and ensure both development and security. It also stressed the need to strengthen leadership teams, while adopting higher standards and taking more concrete measures to advance full and rigorous Party self-governance. The meeting also discussed other matters. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Xiplomacy: Reading Xi's vision for global governance through metaphors
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-23
Xiplomacy: Reading Xi's vision for global governance through metaphors An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 4, 2026 shows a view of the Nanhe water conservancy hub in Xiong'an New Area, north China's Hebei Province. (Xinhua/Mu Yu) BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an) is set to open on Friday in the Xiong'an New Area, north China's Hebei Province, bringing into world focus a pressing question: How can countries work together to address shared challenges in an interconnected world amid growing protectionism and unilateralism? In speeches and meetings on multiple occasions, Chinese President Xi Jinping has used vivid metaphors to articulate his vision for global governance. These metaphors offer insights into his approach to building a more just, equitable and inclusive global governance system. IN SAME BOAT "I was looking at the vast ocean when I boarded the ship, and it struck me that we are all indeed fellow passengers in the same boat," Xi said while addressing the 2018 APEC CEO Summit hosted at a unique setting -- onboard the giant cruise Pacific Explorer in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea. The metaphor embodies the essence of Xi's vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, highlighting the interconnectedness of countries and the need for solidarity and cooperation in addressing common challenges. Today, the interconnected world is grappling with four mounting deficits: a peace deficit that exacerbates geopolitical conflicts, a development deficit that widens the North-South divide, a security deficit that erodes mutual trust, and a governance deficit that undermines the effectiveness of multilateralism. This photo taken on Aug. 30, 2025 shows an exterior view of the main venue of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2025 in Tianjin, north China. (Xinhua/Sun Fanyue) In 2019, at the China-France Global Governance Forum held in Paris, Xi proposed a four-pronged approach to addressing the four deficits. First and foremost, he called for fairness and reasonableness to address the governance deficit. "It is advisable to uphold a vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefits," Xi said, calling for actively advancing the democratization of global governance rules. As the world has found itself in a new period of turbulence and transformation, global governance has come to a new crossroads. Against this backdrop, Xi put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in September 2025 in China's coastal city of Tianjin. "I look forward to working with all countries for a more just and equitable global governance system and advancing toward a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said, stressing sovereign equality and genuine multilateralism. TRAFFIC LIGHTS "A world without rules is like a crossroads without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder are all but guaranteed," Xi said at the 2026 BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India. This metaphor highlights the importance of rules in maintaining the international order. While having rules in place matters, how they are made and who gets to make them matter even more. Media staff work at the media center at Bharat Mandapam, the main venue of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, Sept. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Javed Dar) International rules must be written and upheld jointly by all countries based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, rather than dictated by those with the strongest muscles or the loudest voice, Xi once stressed. He has also called for the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and other universally recognized basic norms of international relations to be observed comprehensively, fully and in their entirety. "There should be no double standards, and the house rules of a few countries must not be imposed upon others," he said. The GGI proposed by President Xi reflects the objective transformation of the world system and responds to the aspirations of most countries for a fairer and more representative system of global governance, said Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University. MAKING THE PIE BIGGER Xi has repeatedly used the metaphor of a pie to describe the gains of international cooperation. "We should make the pie of win-win cooperation bigger, and ensure that more development gains will be shared more fairly by people across the world," he said at the 23rd meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in 2023. The pie metaphor reflects the people-centered and action-oriented vision of the GGI: making the gains of cooperation bigger while ensuring that they are shared more widely and fairly. When proposing the GGI, Xi emphasized the importance of "ensuring that the people of every nation are the actors in and beneficiaries of global governance." Students operate teaching equipment for the artificial intelligence program at the Luban Workshop at L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University in Astana, Kazakhstan, May 22, 2026. (Photo by Kalizhan Ospanov/Xinhua) The SCO, the platform where Xi proposed the GGI, provides an example. Within the grouping, China has announced the establishment of cooperation platforms in energy, green industries and the digital economy, as well as centers for scientific and technological innovation, higher education, and vocational and technical education. The expanding scope of cooperation shows how the "pie" can be made bigger in practice: by opening up new areas of cooperation, creating more opportunities for development and ensuring that the benefits reach more people. Beyond making the pie bigger, Xi has also called for sharing the pie fairly to ensure justice and equity. For him, the ultimate purpose of better global governance is to promote common development and improve people's well-being across the globe. At the G20 summit held in Brazil in 2024, Xi called for building a just world of common development, saying "prosperity and stability would not be possible in a world where the rich become richer while the poor are made poorer, and countries should make global development more inclusive, beneficial to all, and more resilient." To build such a world, Xi said, there should be more bridges of cooperation, and less "small yard, high fences," so that more and more developing countries will be better off and achieve modernization.
